Public Comment: The public is encouraged to address City Council on any matter listed on the agenda or on any other matter
within its jurisdiction subject to the rules of decorum described in Section 2.08.020 of the Norwalk Municipal Code. If you wish to
address City Council, please complete a speaker card and hand the card to the Sergeant at Arms. City Council will hear public
comment on items listed on the agenda during discussion of the matter and prior to a vote and on matters not listed on the agenda
during the Oral Communications period.

Pursuant to provisions of the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the agenda, or unless certain
emergency or special circumstances exist. The City Council may direct staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for
consideration at a future City Council meeting.

Please adhere to the following procedures when addressing the City Council: Comments should be limited to 3 minutes or less
and
directed to the City Council as a whole and not directed to individual Councilmembers.

Americans with Disabilities Act: In compliance with the ADA, if you need special assistance to participate in a City meeting or
other services offered by this City, please contact the City Clerk’s department, (562) 929-5720. Assisted listening devices are
available at this meeting. Ask the City Clerk if you desire to use this device. Upon request, the agenda and documents in the
agenda packet can be made available in appropriate alternative formats to persons with a disability. Notification of at least 48
hours prior to the meeting or time when services are needed will assist the City staff in assuring that reasonable arrangements
can be made to provide accessibility to the meeting or service.

Note: Any writings and/or documents provided to a majority of the City Council regarding any item on this agenda after it has
been posted will also be made available for public inspection. Writings and/or documents are available for inspection in the City
Clerk’s Department, during regular business hours, 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., Monday – Thursday and 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., every
other Friday; telephone (562) 929-5720. You may also contact the City Clerk via e-mail at recordsrequests@norwalkca.gov.

departments for a successful Independence Day Event. Councilmember Ramirez
requested a status update regarding Interstate 105 Freeway and Studebaker Road
involving crash reduction prevention; and wished Councilmember Valencia a Happy
Birthday. Councilmember Rios reported on her attendance at Milagro Cinemas After
Hours Networking Mixer, the Independent Cities Association Summer Seminar, and the
first Summer Concert; expressed concerns about the ongoing immigration issues and
shared that Social Services is increasing services to assist. Councilmember Valencia
reported on her attendance at Media Training and shared concerns regarding the ongoing
immigration issues. Vice Mayor Perez invited all to attend upcoming events such as the
Norwalk Park Planning and Design Community Engagement Meeting being held July 17,
at the Norwalk Arts and Sports Complex; Front Street Friday Nights located on Front
Street, and Dinner and a Movie at the Hargitt House Museum, July 18. Mayor Ayala also
expressed concerns about the ongoing immigration issues and shared that Social
Services has a hotline (562) 929-5961.

improvement projects. Accurate surveying is essential for planning, design, construction, and
infrastructure documentation.

provide City Surveyor and on-call Citywide surveying services. The RFP is for an initial three-

The RFP outlined the City’s need for various surveying tasks, including, Field surveys (tie-outs,
monument verification, grade determination), Quality assurance surveys during construction,
Map checking and legal description certifications.

the submitted proposals based on several factors including technical knowledge, the proposed

Background:

Annually, the Finance department presents to City Council, for consideration and approval,
updates to routine policies as part of ongoing efforts to enhance fiscal responsibility, improve
transparency and ensure alignment with best practices as well as compliance with municipal
code, state and federal requirements.

To ensure policies are updated accordingly, staff are proposing changes to two existing policies,
which are:

  •  Cash Handling Policy
  •  Capitalization Policy

Cash Handling Policy

As part of the City’s commitment to provide excellent customer service, and by extension the
Finance Department’s responsibility to protect public funds, the cash handling policy was
developed and adopted in 2019 to establish the proper and effective internal procedures over
cash handling across the various departments who intake payments as part of day-to-day
operations.

Since the adoption of the policy, staff have been limited to a maximum intake of $5,000 per
transaction when payment is received via credit or debit card. This limitation was implemented
to minimize the impact of the bank credit card processing fees the City would be required to pay
on large transactions. However, on April 1, 2025, the City Council adopted an updated fee
 City Council  August 5, 2025
Fiscal Year 2025/26 Financial Policy Updates  Page No. 2

schedule to take effect July 1, 2025, which includes a 3% credit card processing fee that will be
passed through to the payor and no longer paid by the City.

To minimize the disruption imposed by the existing transaction limitation and allow for a
seamless transition to incorporating the credit card processing fee, an update to the Cash
Handling Policy is required to remove transaction limits for payments accepted by the City.
Exhibit A to Resolution No. 25-33 includes the updated policy removing the credit card
transaction limit.

Capitalization Policy (Fixed Assets)

The Governmental Accounting Standards Board (“GASB”) is responsible for setting accounting
and financial reporting standards for U.S. State and local governments that follow generally
accepted accounting procedures (“GAAP”). One of these standards includes the method in
which governments account for fixed assets, also known as GASB Statement 34 which sets the
reporting requirements of capitalization thresholds, depreciation, disposal of assets and criteria.

In 2003 when GASB statement 34 was established, the minimum capital asset threshold for
capital purchases was set to $5,000 and the Fixed Asset Policy was developed in accordance
with the standards set forth. Since then, various external factors have influenced the cost of
capital outlay purchases, primarily inflation. In an effort to update the Fixed Asset Policy to
account for these changes, as well as remain in compliance with GASB requirements, an update
to the policy is needed. Included as Exhibit A to Resolution No. 25-34 is an updated Fixed Asset
Policy the includes the following changes:

  •  Raising the capitalization threshold from $5,000 to $10,000 in a manner consistent with
  GASB requirements and best practices.
  •  Incorporate additional capital outlay expenditure types.
  •  Removal of obsolete language.

All policies proposed for adoption will become effective following approval by the City Council.

CASH HANDLING PROCESS

Receiving Payment, Counting Cash, and Giving Change

There is a number of ways of counting cash, but the main objective when counting is to
ensure accuracy in receiving cash and giving out proper change to the customer.
Recommended below is the “Hand-to-Table” method of counting to ensure that no bills
and coins are miscounted and the customer acknowledges correct payment and change
(if applicable) from City’s staff.

The “Hand-to-Table” method instruction for counting cash is provided. One may deviate
from this method but whichever method is used to count, recount the money as many
times as necessary to come up with the same total twice. This means you will always
count a stack of currency at least two times. Cash Handlers should also establish a set
routine for counting money.
  7
   Hand-to-Table Method:

  1) Receiving Bills and Coins:

  A. Separate bills into denominations with all the bills facing up. At this time,
  pay special attention to $20, $50, and $100 bills for counterfeits.

  B. If the pile contains more than one denomination, count the largest
  denomination first.

  C. Place the pile in one hand.

  D. Transfer one bill at a time from your hand to the table in the presence of
  the customer.

  E. Check each bill, as you count to ensure correct denomination.

  F. Count all coins received.

  G. Verify the grand total against the amount listed on the billing statement,
  invoice, or Cash Receipt.

  H. If any discrepancies exist, count the money again. If a discrepancy still
  exists, ask the customer to count the money.

  2) Making Change:

  To ensure the accuracy of all transactions, it is important that the cash handler
  follows a routine, accepted practice in making change. There are two ways to give
  change back to a customer.
  • The cash register automatically calculates the dollar amount to be returned
  to the customer, or
  • The cash handler counts from the amount of the sale to the amount
  tendered.

Change should be counted at least two times; once when the cash handler counts it out
of the cash drawer and a second time when the cash handler counts it back to the
customer.

Cash Handler must always give the customer a receipt and put the amount received
in the cash drawer and close the drawer.

At shift closing each cash handler must balance his or her cash drawer. This

i. Losses/Shortages/Overages.

There is a difference between Loss and Shortage of City money, which is
determined by the cash handler’s ability to obtain physical custody of the money
and how that person safeguards the money.

A Shortage is an unintentional collection error such as a change making error. An
Overage occurs when a cash handler has collected too much money and cannot
immediately return the excess to a specific customer.

Cash handler must bring shortage or overage to the attention of the supervisor
who needs to sign off on the shortage or overage amount. No adjustments in
Revenue Management System can be made prior to the supervisor’s approval.

Loss of City money is when a cash handler has obtained physical custody of
money and then due to reasons like negligence, an unlawful action, cannot deposit
that money to the City Treasury.

immediately. Detailed statements as to the circumstances of the Loss, along

CITY OF NORWALK POLICY STATEMENT

Number:  25-03
Subject:  Fixed Asset Policy and Procedures
Adopted Date:  August 5, 2025
Effective Date:  August 5, 2025

BACKGROUND

 The City of Norwalk's fixed asset policy stems from two major objectives: to
 accurately account for and report fixed assets in accordance with generally
 accepted accounting principles and the Governmental Accounting Standards
 Board (GASB), and to assure the safeguarding and preservation of City assets.

 This policy is intended to provide specific guidance for identification, custody,
 capitalization and inventory of asset acquisitions.

 It is the responsibility of the Finance Department to ensure fixed and inventory
 controlled assets will be inventoried on a regular basis and accounted for by fund
 and asset category.

 It is the responsibility of each department to ensure that proper budgeting and
 purchasing guidelines are followed, and to ensure that fixed assets are adequately
 controlled, and safeguarded.

PURPOSE

 To ensure efficient and effective accounting of all fixed assets.  The purpose of
 accounting for the City’s fixed assets is:

  1.  To safeguard the investment in fixed assets.

  2.  To fix responsibility for custody of the equipment

  3.  To provide information for insurance purposes.

  4.  To provide information for financial reporting.

  5.  To account for depreciation of assets.

  6.  To provide historical information for use in the acquisition of future assets
  and the disposition of current assets.

  2
 GENERAL INFORMATION & DEFINITIONS

Assets that are purchased by the City that meet the requirement for a fixed asset or an
inventory-controlled asset are maintained through the Fixed Asset subsystem of
Pentamation. If the assets meet the requirement for a capital asset, annual depreciation
expense will be calculated

  1. Fixed Assets (Capital Asset) – tangible assets having a value of $10,000 these
  items are listed on the inventory registers will be capitalized according to the
  capitalization policy.

  2. Land - The investment in real property other than structures and improvements. It
  does not include land acquired for street and road purposes.

  3. Structures and Improvements - Physical property of a permanent nature such as
  buildings, picnic shelters, storage tanks, reservoirs and parking lots which should
  be capitalized as fixed assets.

  4. Equipment - moveable personal property. Some examples are; furniture,
  machines, tools, vehicles, and typewriters are included in this category.

  a. In some instances, the cost test is applied to aggregates of units of similar
  type or purpose. In the City of Norwalk, the following items are to be
  aggregated: Folding Chairs, Banquet Tables, Shelving and Water Meters

  5. Asset Control Form – This form must be filled out when equipment is
  transferred to another department, sold, abandoned or traded in. As these
  changes take place, they are input in the computer and the property
  records are updated.

  6. Inventory Control Asset - item purchased with a value of $500 but less
  than $10,000 and a useful life of one year. This will be applied to movable
  assets (Vehicles and Equipment) and not to land, buildings or other
  immovable fixed assets. Assets subject to inventory control will be
  accounted for through the same system used to account for fixed assets
  subject to capitalization.

Control Assets.

  1. The Finance Department maintains detailed property records as a
  subsystem of the Pentamation Accounting system, including acquisition
  date; purchase price; description; serial number; department; location and
  3
 funding source.

CAPITALIZATION POLICY

 All fixed assets (Capital Assets), including land, buildings & improvements,
 machinery & equipment, and infrastructure with an original cost of $10,000 or
 more will be subject to capitalization.

There will be no capitalization of construction in process until the project is complete

 All costs associated with the purchase or construction of the asset should be
 considered, including ancillary costs such as freight and transportation
 charges, site preparation expenditures, professional fees, warranties, and legal
 claims directly attributable to the asset acquisition.

 Specific capitalization requirements are:

  1. This capitalization threshold is applied to individual units of fixed assets.

  2. For purposes of capitalization, the threshold will generally not be applied to
  components of fixed assets.

  a. For example, a keyboard, monitor and central processing unit purchases
  as components of a computer system will be treated as a single fixed
  asset.

  3. Donated assets will be recorded at the estimated fair market value at the
  date of acquisition determined by the receiving department.

  4. Subscription based technology agreements (SBITA) and right to use assets
  will be evaluated using $10,000 capitalization threshold.

  5. Purchase of computer software, including software systems, will not be
  capitalized.

  6. Repairs to existing fixed assets will generally not be subject to capitalization
  4
 unless the repair extends the useful life of the asset. In this case, it r epresents
an improvement and is subject to the requirements described below.

  7. Improvements to existing fixed assets that will extend the useful life of the
  related fixed asset will be subject to capitalization only if the cost of the
  improvement meets the $10,000 threshold.

  8. Capital projects will be capitalized as "construction in progress" until
  completed. The costs associated with the capital project include direct
  costs, such as labor and materials, as well as ancillary costs.

  9. Land acquisitions, r i g h t s of way, or easements, are capitalized,
  regardless of cost. Some infrastructure, such as traffic signals, which
  individually may not meet the $10,000 threshold, will be capitalized as a
  "system" rather than an individual asset.

  10. The cost test is applied to aggregates of units of similar type or purpose
  based on the $10,000 threshold. In the City of Norwalk, the following items
  are to be aggregated:

  a. Folding Chairs
  b. Banquet Tables
  c. Shelving
  d. Water Meters

  11. The following items will be evaluated based on the per unit cost rather than
  the aggrege total of the amount of items purchased at one time.

  a. Network items (switches, servers etc.)
  b. Computers (CPU)

  d. Printers

SUBJECT: URGENCY ORDINANCE NO. 25-1758U – AN AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE
  EMERGENCY SHELTERS, SINGLE-ROOM OCCUPANCY, SUPPORTIVE
  HOUSING, AND TRANSITIONAL HOUSING FROM A MORATORIUM AND
  EXTEND THE AMENDED MORATORIUM TO ESTABLISH, IMPLEMENT OR
  OPERATE (TEMPORARILY OR PERMANENTLY) CONVENIENCE STORES
  (LIQUOR  STORES),  DISCOUNT  STORES,  PERSONAL  USE  –
  LAUNDROMATS, VEHICLE/AUTOMOBILE—WASHING, AND PAYDAY LOAN
  ESTABLISHMENTS LOCATED IN THE CITY OF NORWALK FOR ONE
  ADDITIONAL YEAR.

Background:

Urgency Ordinance No. 24-1752U - On August 6, 2024, City Council adopted a 45-day
moratorium to establish, implement, or operate (temporarily or permanently) convenience stores
(liquor stores), discount stores, personal use – laundromat, vehicle/automobile washing, payday
loan establishments, emergency shelters, single-room occupancy, supportive housing, and
transitional housing city-wide (“Moratorium”). Urgency Ordinance No. 24-1752U included a
waiver process for those requesting to establish the listed uses during the Moratorium.

Urgency Ordinance No. 24-1753U - After a 10-day report was received and filed by City Council
on September 3, 2024, the Moratorium was extended on September 17, 2024 for an additional
10 months and 15 days and is set to expire on August 5, 2025, unless extended for an additional
year by City Council pursuant to Government Code Section 65858(a). A maximum of two
extensions of the Moratorium is allowed under Government Section 65858(a).
 City Council  August 5, 2025
Urgency Ordinance No. 25-1758U  Page No. 2

In accordance with Government Code Section 65858(d), prior to City Council consideration of
the second (and final) extension of the Moratorium, a “10-day report” was received and filed by
the City Council on July 15, 2025. The 10-day report described the measures taken to alleviate
the conditions in which led to the adoption of the Moratorium (see Attachment 2).

Amendment to the Moratorium – The current Moratorium includes emergency shelters, single-
room occupancy, supportive housing and transitional housing (“housing uses”) which originated
due to Los Angeles County selecting 12500 Firestone Boulevard for a two-year transitional
housing program without consideration of City and community interests and an exit plan at the
conclusion of the housing program.

Given the poor performance of Project RoomKey in 2021, City Council directed staff to draft an
Urgency Ordinance pursuant to Government Code Section 65858. Since the adoption of the
Moratorium, the City and the County have had productive discussions about utilizing the former
Metro State Hospital located at 11401 Bloomfield Avenue for a shelter instead of 12500 Firestone
Boulevard.

However, as a result of the Moratorium on the housing uses, the California Department of
Housing and Community Development (“HCD”) issued a Notice of Violation and Corrective
Action Letter on September 16, 2024, and after discussions with City staff and HCD, HCD
subsequently revoked the City’s 2021-2029 Housing Element certification on October 2, 2024.

Following this action, the State of California filed a lawsuit against the City on the grounds of
violation of state housing laws. A trial date for the pending litigation is scheduled for October 28,
2025. The City Attorney’s Office and the attorney from the California Attorney General’s Office
have been actively engaged in on-going discussions which may bring resolution to the litigation
and includes the City taking steps to amend the Moratorium to omit emergency shelters, single-
room occupancy, supportive housing, and transitional housing uses. Furthermore, with the goal
of the City having a compliant Housing Element, an amendment of the Moratorium to omit the
above-mentioned housing related uses is necessary. There have been discussions between the
City staff and HCD on the actions and steps necessary to obtain re-certification of the Housing
Element by HCD in an expeditious manner. Urgency Ordinance No. 25-1758U (Attachment 1)
has been prepared to exclude the housing uses.

Extension of the amended Moratorium – As a part of Ordinance No. 25-1758U, a one-year
extension on the moratorium on the establishment, implementation or operation (temporarily or
permanently) of convenience stores (liquor stores), discount store, personal use – laundromats,
vehicle/automobile washing, and payday loan establishments has been prepared for City Council
consideration.

The extension of the amended Moratorium is necessary due to the various uses and issues
studied, additional time is needed for the next steps, which would be for staff to initiate a zoning
code text amendment(s) that will clarify definitions of the aforementioned uses and provide
additional regulations such as development, operational and performance standards.
 City Council  August 5, 2025
Urgency Ordinance No. 25-1758U  Page No. 3

As part of Ordinance No. 25-1758U (which has been carried over from Urgency Ordinances No.
24-1752U and 24-1753U), Section No. 8 outlines a waiver request from the Moratorium. The
Moratorium waiver request can be submitted to the Department of Community Development,
which may be reviewed, approved, or denied administratively or may be subject to review by the
City’s Planning Commission and/or City Council, whose approval or denial shall be within their
sole discretion and constitute the final administrative review of the request for waiver or
exemption of the Urgency Ordinance.
Pursuant to Government Code Section 65858, this extension is final and if adopted, will expire
on August 5, 2026 or until the City Council adopts an ordinance addressing the amended uses
listed in Urgency Ordinance No. 25-1758U, whichever comes first.

Fiscal Impact:

N/A

Citizens Advised:

The public hearing notice was posted at the City’s three designated posting places and
posted online, and the notice was published in The Norwalk Patriot on July 25, 2025.

Strategic Plan 2023 Implementation:

The recommended action will further the City’s Strategic Plan Goals 2 and 3 to work in
partnership with our community to achieve safe and livable neighborhoods and to create and
sustain a resilient and economically prosperous City.

Recommended Action:

Staff recommends City Council adopt Urgency Ordinance No. 25-1758U, AN AMENDMENT TO
EXCLUDE EMERGENCY SHELTERS, SINGLE-ROOM OCCUPANCY, SUPPORTIVE

SUBJECT: PROJECT NO. 7184 - AWARD OF CONTRACT FOR PROFESSIONAL
  SERVICES - STREET DESIGN FOR REHABILITATION OF CARMENITA ROAD
  FROM ROSECRANS AVENUE TO EXCELSIOR DRIVE – ENGINEERS REPORT
  NO. 25-16 AND TERMINATE PROJECT NO. 7904

Background:

On August 5, 2014, City Council awarded a Professional Services Agreement to CNC
Engineering to prepare plans, specifications, and estimates (PS&E) for the rehabilitation of
Carmenita Road from Rosecrans Avenue to the Interstate 5 Freeway (Project No. 7184). The
scope of work included pavement analysis, survey services, Americans with Disablity Act (ADA)-
compliant curb ramp and bus stop improvements, drainage evaluation, and sidewalk gap
closures, with the intent of preparing the corridor for increased traffic volumes anticipated from
the future completion of the Carmenita Bridge widening project by Caltrans.

Although the design was finalized by CNC Engineering, the project did not proceed to
construction at the time due to budgetary constraints.

Since then, Carmenita Bridge has been completed, resulting in increased traffic volumes and
heavier vehicle loads on this section of Carmenita Road. Additionally, the original PS&E package
is now over a decade old and does not reflect current field conditions, updated design standards,
or the increased traffic impacts observed since the bridge’s completion.

the City’s pre-qualified on-call design firms to secure updated design services for the Carmenita
Road improvements from Rosecrans Avenue to Excelsior Drive under Project No. 7184.

On June 17, 2025, the City received proposals from five firms from pre-qualified engineering
firms to provide design services for project No 7184.

Staff examined and reviewed the submitted proposals based on several factors including

Background

On July 5, 2024, City Council awarded a contract to Transtech Engineers, Inc. in the amount of
$159,235 for Construction Management and Inspection (CM&I) services for Traffic Signal
Improvements on Alondra Boulevard between the Home Depot Signal and Shoemaker Avenue;
Project No. 7232. The CM&I services include management and inspections of upgrades to traffic
signal hardware, installations of new pedestrian countdown signal heads, updates to the signal
timing coordination at specific locations along the entire corridors, and coordination with
Southern California Edison for required meter relocations.

On November 6, 2024, City Council approved Amendment No. 1 to continue the scope of work
of Construction Management and Inspection Services for Project No. 7232 in an amount not to
exceed $53,999. The project construction phase reached substantial completion in November
2024. Amendment No. 2, in an amount not to exceed $7,092, is required to extend the
performance period of the current professional services agreement to provide coverage through
substantial completion and project close out.

Engineering, Inc. in the amount of $1,579,769 for Traffic Signal Improvements on Studebaker
Road from Kenney Street to Rosecrans Avenue. A contingency in the amount of $333,063 was
included for the subject project.

The project provides upgrades to traffic signal hardware, installation of new pedestrian
countdown signal heads, install American with Disabilities Act (ADA) compliant curb ramps, and
updates signal timing coordination at specific locations along the entire project corridor.

by the City, unforeseen conditions, and design discrepancies. The final project cost is
$1,912,832.

The project was completed satisfactorily on February 18, 2025.
